title: Ezekiel 39:11–20
context: The LORD says Gog will be buried in Israel, in a valley east of the sea that will be called the valley of Hamon Gog. The house of Israel will spend seven months burying the dead to cleanse the land, with men appointed to search for remains, and a city will be named Hamonah. The LORD then tells Ezekiel to summon the birds and animals to a great “sacrifice” on the mountains of Israel, a feast on the defeated armies. The scene is a vivid image of judgment that reverses ordinary sacrifice, comparable to Isaiah 34:6 and Zephaniah 1:7, and later echoed in Revelation 19:17–18. The place names and the numbers are uncertain and may be symbolic.

verses.text: “ ‘ “It will happen in that day, that I will give to Gog a place for burial in Israel, the valley of those who pass through on the east of the sea; and it will stop those who pass through. They will bury Gog and all his multitude there, and they will call it ‘The valley of Hamon Gog’.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will give Gog a burial place in Israel, in “the valley of those who pass through,” east of the sea, to be called “The valley of Hamon Gog.” The invader is buried in the land he attacked.

Arminian readers see the end of the threat.
verses.reformedNotes:
The location is uncertain, and the name seems to mean something like the multitude of Gog, though readers differ.

Reformed readers see God’s victory memorialized. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the place hedged.

verses.text: “ ‘ “The house of Israel will be burying them for seven months, that they may cleanse the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
The house of Israel will bury the dead for seven months to cleanse the land. The work is long and careful.

Arminian readers see the people taking part in restoring the land’s purity after God’s victory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Contact with the dead brought uncleanness under the law (compare Numbers 19:11, 16), which may explain the concern for cleansing. The seven months may be literal or symbolic.

Reformed readers see holiness restored. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Yes, all the people of the land will bury them; and they will become famous in the day that I will be glorified,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the people of the land will bury them and become famous on the day the LORD is glorified. The burial is a shared task.

Arminian readers see the people honored for their part in cleansing the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
The renown seems tied to God’s glory rather than to Israel’s military success.

Reformed readers see the people sharing in God’s glory. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s people reflecting his honor, with the victory itself attributed to God and not to them.

verses.text: “ ‘ “They will set apart men of continual employment who will pass through the land. Those who pass through will go with those who bury those who remain on the surface of the land, to cleanse it. After the end of seven months they will search.
verses.arminianNotes:
Men will be set apart to pass through the land and bury those remaining on the surface; after seven months they will search. The cleansing is thorough.

Arminian readers see diligent obedience in completing the work.
verses.reformedNotes:
The description suggests an organized effort to leave no remains behind; the details are hard to reconstruct.

Reformed readers see the seriousness of the land’s purity. Both traditions read this as shared ground about thoroughness in removing what defiles.

verses.text: Those who search through the land will pass through; and when anyone sees a man’s bone, then he will set up a sign by it, until the undertakers have buried it in the valley of Hamon Gog.
verses.arminianNotes:
When anyone sees a human bone, he will set up a marker until the buriers take it to the valley of Hamon Gog. Even a single bone matters.

Arminian readers see careful attention to purity.
verses.reformedNotes:
The marker would warn others and guide the buriers.

Reformed readers see holiness extending to every part of the land. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the care taken to cleanse the land, described here soberly and without dwelling on the dead.

verses.text: Hamonah will also be the name of a city. Thus they will cleanse the land.” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
“Hamonah will also be the name of a city.” Thus they will cleanse the land. The cleansing is complete.

Arminian readers see a memorial of God’s victory and the land made clean once more.
verses.reformedNotes:
The name Hamonah seems related to Hamon Gog, but the text gives no further details, and its location or symbolic sense is uncertain.

Reformed readers see God’s work remembered. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the identification hedged.

verses.text: “You, son of man, the Lord GOD says: ‘Speak to the birds of every sort, and to every animal of the field, “Assemble yourselves, and come; gather yourselves on every side to my sacrifice that I sacrifice for you, even a great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel, that you may eat meat and drink blood.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD tells Ezekiel to summon the birds and animals to “my sacrifice,” a great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel. The defeat is pictured as a sacrificial meal.

Arminian readers see a judgment image, not a literal rite.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image reverses ordinary sacrifice: the defeated armies become the offering. Compare Isaiah 34:6 and Zephaniah 1:7, where the LORD “has prepared a sacrifice.”

Reformed readers see God’s judgment portrayed vividly. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: You shall eat the flesh of the mighty, and drink the blood of the princes of the earth, of rams, of lambs, and of goats, of bulls, all of them fatlings of Bashan.
verses.arminianNotes:
The guests will eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth, pictured as rams, lambs, goats, and bulls of Bashan. The leaders are portrayed as sacrificial animals.

Arminian readers see proud rulers humbled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Bashan was known for fine livestock, so the image stresses the prominence of those judged.

Reformed readers see God humbling the powerful. Both traditions read this as shared ground and read the image as poetic judgment language.

verses.text: You shall eat fat until you are full, and drink blood until you are drunk, of my sacrifice which I have sacrificed for you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The guests will eat and drink to the full at the sacrifice the LORD has prepared. The feast is complete.

Arminian readers see the image underlining the totality of the defeat, not inviting fascination with it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Under the law Israel was forbidden to eat fat or blood (compare Leviticus 3:17), which may sharpen the reversal in this image.

Reformed readers see the thoroughness of God’s judgment. Both traditions read this as shared ground and read the language soberly.

verses.text: You shall be filled at my table with horses and charioteers, with mighty men, and with all men of war,” says the Lord GOD.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The guests will be filled at the LORD’s table with horses, charioteers, mighty men, and all men of war. The feast scene closes.

Arminian readers see military might brought to nothing before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Revelation 19:17–18 later uses similar imagery for “the great supper of God.” Readers differ on how the two passages relate.

Reformed readers see God’s victory over every power. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep the imagery sober.
